questions.stem: What are the three principal functions of the lymphatic system emphasized in Chapter 22?

choices.text: Return tissue fluid to blood, support immune defense, and transport absorbed intestinal fats
Return fluid directly to arteries, initiate immunity, and deliver lipids mainly through portal blood
Produce antibodies in lymphatic vessels, recirculate red blood cells, and move dietary fat into bile
Return interstitial fluid to capillaries, carry all dietary nutrients through lymph, and eliminate immune surveillance

questions.explanation: The anatomy lecture names fluid recovery, immune response, and fat absorption as the three major functions.

questions.stem: A patient develops swelling after lymph vessels are surgically damaged. Which mechanism best explains the swelling?

choices.text: Interstitial fluid is not being returned to the blood efficiently
Capillary filtration into the damaged tissue has ceased completely
Local venous return increases enough to remove all extracellular fluid
Protein-rich fluid is cleared more rapidly despite the lymphatic obstruction

questions.explanation: Blocked lymphatic return can accumulate fluid in tissues, producing lymphedema.

questions.stem: A fluid sample is taken from between muscle cells and then from an adjacent lymphatic vessel. What changes in its name?

choices.text: It is called interstitial fluid in tissue and lymph inside the lymphatic vessel
The fluid is lymph in tissue spaces and becomes interstitial fluid after entering a vessel
The fluid is called plasma in tissue spaces and lymph inside a blood venule
The names are interchangeable regardless of where the fluid is located

questions.explanation: The names describe the fluid's compartment; entry to a lymphatic vessel makes it lymph.

questions.stem: Why is the lymphatic system important to maintaining blood volume?

choices.text: It returns part of the fluid filtered out of blood capillaries to the venous circulation
It provides the pressure that pumps blood from the heart through arteries
It prevents any filtration of plasma water out of blood capillaries
It replaces the venous circulation as the main return path for whole blood

questions.explanation: Lymphatic fluid recovery supports normal circulation by returning interstitial fluid.

questions.stem: Which situation would most directly increase interstitial edema despite normal heart pumping?

choices.text: Obstruction of local collecting lymphatics
Increased lymphatic outflow from that tissue
Faster removal of interstitial protein and water
Reduced capillary filtration coupled with normal drainage

questions.explanation: Edema can arise when local fluid entry exceeds lymphatic removal.

questions.stem: After a meal rich in long-chain triglycerides, which fluid may have a milky appearance?

choices.text: Chyle in intestinal lymphatics
Venous plasma in the lower limb after ordinary fasting
Lymph draining the lungs before any intestinal lipid absorption
Interstitial fluid in muscles that does not contain absorbed lipoproteins

questions.explanation: Chyle is lymph enriched in chylomicrons, which can make it appear milky.

questions.stem: Which pressure generally promotes movement of water outward across blood capillaries?

choices.text: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
Plasma oncotic pressure exerted by circulating albumin
Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure acting toward the capillary
A reduced capillary pressure relative to the surrounding interstitium

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure helps drive filtration toward surrounding tissues.

questions.stem: Which statement best connects lymphatic and circulatory anatomy?

choices.text: Lymph ultimately returns to venous blood near the junctions of jugular and subclavian veins
Every lymphatic empties into an artery near the tissue it drains
Lymphatic capillaries drain directly into the aorta
Lymph is permanently isolated from the blood circulation

questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage completes a fluid-return loop into venous circulation.

questions.stem: Which structural difference helps initial lymphatic capillaries take up interstitial fluid?

choices.text: Their overlapping endothelial cells form pressure-sensitive entry flaps
A thick, continuous basement membrane that prevents protein entry
Rigid endothelial tight junctions that never change with tissue pressure
A continuous muscular wall that generates high intraluminal suction

questions.explanation: Overlapping endothelial edges favor inward entry from tissue.

questions.stem: Why are initial lymphatic capillaries described as blind-ended?

choices.text: They begin as closed-end pockets in tissues rather than forming blood-capillary loops
They connect artery to vein without branches
They carry no fluid unless a heart is attached
They terminate in the liver's bile ducts

questions.explanation: Initial lymphatics start as blind-ended uptake structures.

questions.stem: What happens when tissue pressure rises outside a lymphatic capillary?

choices.text: Entry flaps can open to admit fluid and anchoring filaments can help prevent collapse
The flaps close more tightly so fluid is retained in the tissue
Fluid exits the lymphatic capillary directly through the open flaps
Only collecting-vessel valves change, while initial capillary entry remains unaffected

questions.explanation: Tissue pressure can favor inward uptake; anchoring filaments support capillary patency.

questions.stem: Why do collecting lymphatic vessels contain many valves?

choices.text: Their low-pressure flow requires protection against backflow
They must reverse direction after each heartbeat
Valves produce antibody proteins
Lymph must remain trapped in the limbs

questions.explanation: Valves maintain net one-way transport despite intermittent compression and low pressure.

questions.stem: A person walks after sitting immobile for hours. Why might lymph return from the legs improve?

choices.text: Muscle contractions compress collecting vessels and valves direct the fluid centrally
Skeletal muscle relaxation creates an equal pressure throughout every collecting vessel
Movement closes all valves simultaneously and stops lymph transport
Leg-muscle contraction forces lymph outward into surrounding tissues

questions.explanation: The skeletal-muscle pump assists movement past one-way valves.

questions.stem: How does breathing support lymph drainage?

choices.text: Changes in thoracic and abdominal pressure help draw and propel lymph centrally
Breathing increases abdominal pressure without changing thoracic pressure
Thoracic pressure changes reverse the one-way valves after each breath
Respiratory movements directly pump lymph out of venous blood back into tissues

questions.explanation: Pressure gradients generated by respiration supplement collecting-vessel contraction.

questions.stem: Where would chylomicrons first enter the lymphatic network after leaving intestinal epithelial cells?

choices.text: Lacteals within small-intestinal villi
Renal glomeruli
Thymic medullary sinuses
The splenic artery

questions.explanation: Lacteals specialize in receiving intestinal lipid particles.

questions.stem: Which statement about lymphatic pumping is most accurate?

choices.text: Flow uses valves, body movement, breathing, and rhythmic collecting-vessel contraction without a single heart-like pump
A central pump creates arterial-level pressure throughout collecting lymphatics
External movements alone propel lymph; collecting-vessel walls cannot contract
The flow relies on passive diffusion with no role for valves or pressure changes

questions.explanation: Multiple distributed mechanisms drive low-pressure lymph return.

questions.stem: Which territory usually drains toward the right lymphatic duct?

choices.text: Right head and neck, right upper limb, and right thorax
Entire left lower limb and pelvis
Both lower limbs and all abdominal organs
Left head and neck, left arm, and left thorax

questions.explanation: The right upper quadrant is the usual right lymphatic duct territory.

questions.stem: Which duct returns lymph from most of the body?

choices.text: Thoracic duct
Right lymphatic duct
Common bile duct
Pancreatic duct

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct drains both lower quadrants and the left upper quadrant.

questions.stem: Which three named trunks are the key inputs for the right lymphatic duct in the lecture?

choices.text: Right jugular, right subclavian, right bronchomediastinal
Right lumbar, left lumbar, intestinal
Left jugular, left subclavian, left bronchomediastinal
Right hepatic, cystic, pancreatic

questions.explanation: The right upper quadrant uses the right-sided jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks.

questions.stem: Which three trunks commonly converge near the cisterna chyli in the class diagram?

choices.text: Right lumbar, left lumbar, and intestinal trunks
Both jugular trunks and the right subclavian trunk
Both bronchomediastinal trunks and the left jugular trunk
Both pulmonary veins and the portal vein

questions.explanation: Lumbar and intestinal trunks collect inferior-body and intestinal lymph.

questions.stem: A lymphatic tracer enters the LEFT foot. Which route is appropriate?

choices.text: Left lumbar drainage toward cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, then left venous angle
Left leg → left jugular trunk → right lymphatic duct → right venous angle
Left leg → right subclavian trunk → right lymphatic duct → right venous angle
Left leg → left lumbar trunk → right lymphatic duct → right venous angle

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct returns lymph from both lower limbs.

questions.stem: Where does the thoracic duct usually terminate?

choices.text: Near the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins
Right ventricle of the heart
Abdominal aorta
Main pancreatic duct

questions.explanation: The usual terminal site is the left venous angle.

questions.stem: Which structure is an expanded chamber near the inferior start of the thoracic duct?

choices.text: Cisterna chyli
Lymph node paracortex
Hassall corpuscle
Medullary cord

questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from lumbar and intestinal territories.

questions.stem: Which trunk normally collects lymph from an upper limb?

choices.text: Subclavian trunk on that side
Intestinal trunk
Lumbar trunk exclusively
Cystic duct

questions.explanation: The right and left subclavian trunks drain their respective upper limbs.

questions.stem: Which lymphatic vessels convey lymph INTO a lymph node?

choices.text: Afferent lymphatic vessels
Efferent lymphatic vessels
Splenic veins
Hepatic portal veins

questions.explanation: Afferent means arriving at a node; efferent means leaving.

questions.stem: Where does lymph first arrive inside a typical node after entering via afferent vessels?

choices.text: Subcapsular sinus
Germinal center only
Thymic medulla
Splenic red pulp

questions.explanation: The subcapsular sinus receives incoming lymph beneath the capsule.

questions.stem: Which region of a lymph node is particularly enriched in B-cell follicles?

choices.text: Outer cortex
Paracortex exclusively
Hilum
Medullary sinus exclusively

questions.explanation: Follicles are characteristic of the outer cortex.

questions.stem: Where are many T lymphocytes concentrated in a lymph node?

choices.text: Paracortex (deep cortex)
Capsular connective tissue
Afferent lymphatic lumen
Splenic red pulp

questions.explanation: The paracortex is a T-cell-rich zone.

questions.stem: What is the principal activity of a germinal center during a response?

choices.text: Activated B-cell proliferation and affinity-related selection
Activated T cells mature into red-pulp macrophages inside follicles
Naïve B cells leave the node without proliferation or differentiation
T cells undergo thymic positive and negative selection inside the germinal center

questions.explanation: Germinal centers support B-cell proliferation and maturation after activation.

questions.stem: Which sequence is closest to the physical pathway of LYMPH through a node?

choices.text: Afferent vessel → subcapsular sinus → cortical/medullary sinuses → efferent vessel
Afferent vessel → thymic medulla → spleen → artery
Efferent vessel → germinal center → afferent vessel → capillary
Splenic artery → medullary cord → jugular trunk

questions.explanation: Fluid travels through sinus spaces; the B-cell and T-cell regions are nearby immune compartments.

questions.stem: What is the functional advantage of bringing antigen and lymphocytes into lymph nodes?

choices.text: It facilitates antigen sampling and encounters among antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes
It ensures that every lymphocyte recognizes every antigen equally
It replaces the need for T-cell costimulation and innate signaling
It prevents all antigens from leaving the subcapsular sinus

questions.explanation: Nodes both filter lymph and coordinate adaptive activation.

questions.stem: How can circulating naive lymphocytes enter a lymph node without arriving in afferent lymph?

choices.text: Through specialized high endothelial venules
Through afferent lymphatics exclusively, never directly from blood
Through large arterial branches opening directly into the follicular cortex
Through efferent lymphatics by reverse flow into the paracortex

questions.explanation: High endothelial venules allow lymphocyte entry from the blood.

questions.stem: Where do human B lymphocytes normally develop and mature?

choices.text: Bone marrow
Thymic medulla
Splenic red pulp exclusively
Thoracic duct

questions.explanation: B cells are bone-marrow-derived; their later activation may occur in secondary lymphoid tissues.

questions.stem: Where do T lymphocytes mature and undergo selection?

choices.text: Thymus
Bone marrow exclusively
Liver bile ducts
Lacteals

questions.explanation: T-cell precursors originate from marrow but mature in the thymus.

questions.stem: Which lymphocyte class belongs primarily to innate defense?

choices.text: Natural killer cells
Antigen-specific memory B cells
Naive CD4 helper T cells
Plasma cells

questions.explanation: NK cells act through innate surveillance and killing.

questions.stem: Which pair are the principal antigen-specific adaptive lymphocyte classes?

choices.text: B cells and T cells
Erythrocytes and platelets
Neutrophils and eosinophils
Macrophages and mast cells exclusively

questions.explanation: B and T lymphocytes use clonally generated antigen receptors and can form memory.

questions.stem: What is the central purpose of the blood–thymus barrier, particularly in the cortex?

choices.text: Limit premature exposure of developing thymocytes to circulating antigens
Keep all circulating antigens permanently inside the thymus medulla
Prevent thymic epithelial cells from contacting immature thymocytes
Completely separate thymocytes from self-antigen presentation during selection

questions.explanation: The barrier supports the developing thymocyte environment.

questions.stem: Why does thymic negative selection matter?

choices.text: It helps remove or control developing T cells that strongly recognize self-antigens
Eliminate all thymocytes that recognize self-MHC at any strength
Guarantee that every mature T cell can react against all tissue antigens
Select cells only for the ability to secrete antibodies in the thymus

questions.explanation: Strong self-reactivity is a danger for autoimmune responses.

questions.stem: Which process favors survival of thymocytes capable of recognizing self-MHC sufficiently?

choices.text: Positive selection
Opsonization
Complement lysis
Chylomicron formation

questions.explanation: Positive selection establishes functional MHC recognition; negative selection addresses excessive self-reactivity.

questions.stem: What is thymic involution?

choices.text: Age-related reduction of thymic lymphoid tissue with replacement by fatty/connective tissue
Sudden conversion of the spleen into a thymus
Lifelong enlargement of the thymus in every adult
Flow of lymph from intestine directly through thymic cortex

questions.explanation: Involution reduces thymic volume over time but does not imply that all immune defenses disappear.

questions.stem: How does splenic immune surveillance differ fundamentally from lymph-node surveillance?

choices.text: Spleen primarily filters blood, whereas lymph nodes primarily filter lymph
Spleen chiefly filters lymph; lymph nodes chiefly filter circulating blood
Both filter circulating blood equally, but only lymph nodes contain immune cells
Spleen and lymph nodes both receive antigen primarily through afferent lymphatic vessels

questions.explanation: The spleen responds to blood-borne antigens and removes abnormal blood cells.

questions.stem: Which splenic compartment is enriched in lymphocytes and immune responses to blood antigens?

choices.text: White pulp
Red pulp exclusively
Hilum
Splenic capsule alone

questions.explanation: White pulp is lymphocyte-rich.

questions.stem: Which splenic compartment is associated with removal of damaged or senescent red blood cells?

choices.text: Red pulp
White pulp exclusively
Afferent lymphatic sinus
Peyer's patch

questions.explanation: Red pulp is blood-rich and contains macrophages that clear old or abnormal RBCs.

questions.stem: What enters and leaves the spleen at its hilum?

choices.text: Splenic artery and vein
Splenic artery and thoracic duct
Afferent and efferent lymphatics forming the node-like sinus system
Portal vein and hepatic artery

questions.explanation: The hilum is the major vascular gateway of the spleen.

questions.stem: What happens to iron from many aged red blood cells removed by splenic macrophages?

choices.text: It can be recovered and recycled for future hemoglobin synthesis
It is all eliminated without reuse when hemoglobin is degraded
It is retained inside splenic macrophages and never enters circulation again
It is converted directly into bilirubin and cannot be used for new hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Macrophages help recover iron from hemoglobin.

questions.stem: Which surface of the spleen conforms to the diaphragm?

choices.text: Diaphragmatic surface
Visceral surface with gastric impressions
Thymic cortex
Medullary sinus

questions.explanation: The smooth outer diaphragmatic surface is a gross anatomical landmark.

questions.stem: Which consequence is clinically important after removal of the spleen?

choices.text: Increased susceptibility to severe infections by some encapsulated bacteria
Loss of circulating lymphocytes because no T cells can mature outside the spleen
A complete loss of antigen-specific immune memory after splenectomy
Reduced defenses against encapsulated bacteria because all lymph nodes stop working

questions.explanation: Splenic clearance of certain blood-borne encapsulated microbes is especially valuable.

questions.stem: Why can trauma to the spleen be medically dangerous?

choices.text: Its highly vascular tissue can bleed extensively into the abdomen
The spleen lacks a connective-tissue capsule and therefore always ruptures
Its thin-walled sinusoids contain no blood until after a traumatic injury
A ruptured spleen primarily blocks lymph drainage without causing bleeding

questions.explanation: Splenic injury can cause major internal hemorrhage and shock.

questions.stem: Which characteristic distinguishes the three encapsulated lymphoid organs named in the instructor's comparison?

choices.text: They have a recognizable connective-tissue capsule
They have no contact with immune cells
They all produce red cells throughout life
They only exist in the intestinal wall

questions.explanation: The course lists nodes, thymus, and spleen as encapsulated organs.

questions.stem: Which pair is usually classified as PRIMARY lymphoid sites for lymphocyte development?

choices.text: Bone marrow and thymus
Lymph node and spleen
Palatine tonsil and Peyer's patch
Appendix and thoracic duct

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns lymphocyte maturation, not merely the presence of a capsule.

questions.stem: What is the principal location of Peyer's patches?

choices.text: Small intestine, especially the ileum
Thymic medulla
Left atrium of the heart
Renal cortex

questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated intestinal lymphoid follicles.

questions.stem: Where is the pharyngeal tonsil located?

choices.text: Roof/posterior wall of the nasopharynx
Lower abdomen near appendix
Splenic hilum
Pancreatic head

questions.explanation: The pharyngeal tonsil is the adenoid region.

questions.stem: Which tissue grouping helps protect mucosal surfaces such as gut and airways?

choices.text: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT)
Splenic red pulp only
Bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells only
The lymphangion wall

questions.explanation: MALT positions immune cells near surfaces exposed to external material.

questions.stem: What does GALT stand for?

choices.text: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue
Germinal artery lymph transport
Glomerular antigen liver tissue
Gastric acid luminal transport

questions.explanation: GALT is the intestinal/mucosal component of the lymphoid system.

questions.stem: Which collection of tissue surrounds the opening of the pharynx?

choices.text: Waldeyer's ring of tonsillar lymphoid tissue
Thoracic duct and lumbar trunks
Splenic red pulp cords
Pancreatic islets

questions.explanation: Waldeyer's ring includes palatine, pharyngeal, and lingual tonsillar tissues.

questions.stem: What is the immunological role of specialized intestinal M cells?

choices.text: Transport antigens from the intestinal lumen toward underlying mucosal immune tissue
Create erythrocytes in the intestinal epithelium
Secrete hydrochloric acid into the stomach
Produce all circulating IgG

questions.explanation: M cells help sample luminal antigen near intestinal immune follicles.

questions.stem: Which is the instructor's exact group of seven nonspecific defense categories?

choices.text: Physical barriers, phagocytic cells, immunological surveillance, interferons, complement, inflammation, fever
B cells, plasma cells, helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells, antibodies, memory, tolerance
Lymph, chyle, blood, marrow, thymus, spleen, tonsils
Mastication, absorption, secretion, compaction, defecation, filtration, digestion

questions.explanation: These seven named categories are explicitly listed in the Chapter 22 immunity lecture.

questions.stem: A bacterium crosses broken skin. Which action represents an immediate cellular innate defense?

choices.text: Neutrophils and macrophages engulf microbial material
Naive B cells immediately secrete class-switched IgG without activation
All T cells become antibodies
The thoracic duct directly neutralizes the bacterium

questions.explanation: Phagocytes respond without requiring prior specific antigen exposure.

questions.stem: Which immune cell is specialized to capture antigen and help activate naive T cells?

choices.text: Dendritic cell
Erythrocyte
Platelet
Intestinal enterocyte

questions.explanation: Dendritic cells connect early antigen capture to adaptive antigen presentation.

questions.stem: Which description best fits an NK cell?

choices.text: Innate lymphocyte able to kill some virus-infected or tumor-like abnormal cells
Antibody-producing terminal B cell
Cell whose defining role is making red blood cells
Liver cell making bile

questions.explanation: NK cells provide cytotoxic immunological surveillance.

questions.stem: A target cell has reduced surface MHC class I expression. Which cell type may respond through missing-self recognition?

choices.text: Natural killer cell
Plasma cell producing IgA
Mature red blood cell
Chylomicron

questions.explanation: Some NK receptors use the absence of inhibitory self-MHC signals as part of target assessment.

questions.stem: How do perforin and granzymes collaborate in cytotoxic killing?

choices.text: Perforin helps granzyme entry, and granzymes trigger cell-death pathways
They neutralize stomach acid to protect the intestine
They assemble immunoglobulin heavy chains
They produce lymphatic valves around a target cell

questions.explanation: NK cells and CD8 T cells use cytotoxic granule proteins to trigger apoptosis.

questions.stem: What is a major difference between NK and CD8 cytotoxic T-cell recognition?

choices.text: NK cells use innate activating/inhibitory cues, while CD8 T cells recognize specific peptide–MHC I complexes
NK cells alone require rearranged T-cell receptors
CD8 T cells never kill infected cells
Both depend on circulating antibody as their only recognition mechanism

questions.explanation: Their killing machinery can overlap, but antigen recognition differs.

questions.stem: Which statement is most precise about the word 'nonspecific' in innate immunity?

choices.text: Innate pathways recognize conserved threat patterns but do not use the same highly diversified receptors as adaptive lymphocytes
Innate cells cannot distinguish any molecules at all
Innate defenses only work after vaccination
Innate immunity excludes inflammatory signaling

questions.explanation: 'Nonspecific' is the classroom category; recognition is still biologically selective.

questions.stem: Which classical sign of inflammation means redness?

choices.text: Rubor
Calor
Tumor
Dolor

questions.explanation: Rubor is redness, commonly from increased local perfusion.

questions.stem: Which classical sign of inflammation means swelling?

choices.text: Tumor
Calor
Dolor
Rubor

questions.explanation: Tumor is swelling in the Latin list of inflammatory signs, not automatically a neoplasm.

questions.stem: Which classical sign of inflammation means heat?

choices.text: Calor
Rubor
Dolor
Tumor

questions.explanation: Calor corresponds to warmth at the inflamed site.

questions.stem: Which classical sign of inflammation means pain?

choices.text: Dolor
Calor
Tumor
Rubor

questions.explanation: Dolor is pain associated with tissue injury and inflammatory mediators.

questions.stem: Why does histamine often promote visible local swelling?

choices.text: It can increase vascular permeability so more fluid enters tissues
It seals all capillaries against fluid movement
It converts interstitial fluid into red cells
It inhibits all local blood flow

questions.explanation: Mast-cell mediators alter microvascular permeability and perfusion.

questions.stem: How do neutrophils reach inflamed tissues from nearby blood vessels?

choices.text: Through regulated adhesion, extravasation, and chemotactic migration
By converting into platelets and entering lymph ducts
By traveling only inside neurons
By passing backward through pancreatic ducts

questions.explanation: Leukocytes leave blood vessels and follow inflammatory chemical gradients.

questions.stem: What is a pyrogen's relationship to fever?

choices.text: It helps raise the regulated temperature set point through inflammatory signaling
It directly lowers all tissue temperature below normal
It supplies oxygen to lymph nodes
It converts antibodies into cytokines

questions.explanation: Pyrogenic signaling involves the hypothalamus and prostaglandin pathways.

questions.stem: Why can a person feel cold and shiver while developing a fever?

choices.text: The body's thermoregulatory set point has risen above current temperature
All blood vessels have become permanently paralyzed
Their thymus is producing excessive chyle
Antibodies have stopped working in all tissues

questions.explanation: Raising the set point can trigger heat-conserving and heat-generating responses.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment is a major opsonin?

choices.text: C3b
IgD
Perforin
Thymosin

questions.explanation: C3b coats targets, improving phagocytic uptake.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the membrane attack complex?

choices.text: Form pores that can damage certain target-cell membranes
Transport fatty acids from intestine to lymph
Mature developing T cells in the thymus
Attach lymph nodes to the diaphragm

questions.explanation: The MAC, assembled from terminal complement proteins, can perforate susceptible membranes.

questions.stem: Which complement route can be triggered by antibodies bound to antigen?

choices.text: Classical pathway
Intestinal absorption pathway
Thymic positive selection
Intrinsic lymphatic pump

questions.explanation: The classical complement pathway often follows antigen–antibody complex formation.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway responds to microbial carbohydrate signatures?

choices.text: Lectin pathway
T-cell receptor rearrangement
Secretory IgD pathway
Portal vein pathway

questions.explanation: Lectin-mediated recognition can initiate complement without preexisting specific antibody.

questions.stem: What is opsonization?

choices.text: Coating a pathogen so phagocytes recognize and ingest it more efficiently
Direct formation of lymph in the spleen
The elimination of all self-reactive thymocytes
The transfer of chylomicrons through milk

questions.explanation: IgG and C3b are common opsonins.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment is a potent signal for inflammatory-cell recruitment?

choices.text: C5a
Hemoglobin
Thymosin
Antibody light chain

questions.explanation: C5a is a strong anaphylatoxin/chemoattractant in complement activation.

questions.stem: How do type I interferons help defend neighboring cells from viruses?

choices.text: They induce cellular antiviral programs that can inhibit viral replication
They physically carry viruses to the kidney for filtration
They become IgM molecules in plasma
They replace all lymphocyte antigen receptors

questions.explanation: Infection-induced interferon signaling can make cells less permissive to replication.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts neutralization and opsonization?

choices.text: Neutralization blocks harmful interactions; opsonization tags a target for engulfment
Both are names for lymph duct drainage
Neutralization means T-cell apoptosis; opsonization means fever
Opsonization prevents receptor binding while neutralization always creates pores

questions.explanation: Antibodies can act by different effector mechanisms, including both blocking and tagging.

questions.stem: Which MHC class is normally expressed by nearly all nucleated cells?

choices.text: MHC class I
MHC class II only
Immunoglobulin E
C3b

questions.explanation: Class I MHC broadly displays intracellularly derived peptides.

questions.stem: Which pairing is the standard exam association?

choices.text: MHC I with CD8 cytotoxic T cells
MHC I with secreted IgA
MHC II with CD8 cytotoxic T cells exclusively
MHC II with red blood cells as professional presenters

questions.explanation: CD8 recognizes class I; CD4 helper T cells recognize class II.

questions.stem: Which pairing is the standard exam association for helper T cells?

choices.text: MHC II with CD4 helper T cells
MHC II with CD8 cytotoxic T cells exclusively
IgG with neutrophil MHC IV
MHC I with platelet-derived antibodies

questions.explanation: CD4 helper cells respond to peptides presented on MHC II.

questions.stem: Which cell is normally a professional MHC II antigen-presenting cell?

choices.text: Dendritic cell
Mature erythrocyte
Intestinal chylomicron
Smooth muscle fiber

questions.explanation: Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells can display antigen on MHC II.

questions.stem: What must a naive T cell often receive in addition to antigen recognition for appropriate activation?

choices.text: Costimulatory signals
A chylomicron
A blood-thymus barrier around each node
A lymphatic valve opening outward

questions.explanation: A second activation signal helps avoid inappropriate responses.

questions.stem: What is the chief result of activating an appropriate CD8 cytotoxic T cell?

choices.text: Expansion of cells able to recognize and eliminate target cells bearing its peptide–MHC I antigen
Immediate conversion of the T cell into a plasma cell
Direct release of all antibodies from the thymus
Permanent closure of lymphatic capillaries

questions.explanation: Antigen-specific CTLs can kill infected or abnormal target cells and form memory.

questions.stem: What is a key role of CD4 helper T cells in antibody-mediated defense?

choices.text: Provide activation signals and cytokine support to appropriate B cells
Become the heavy chains of secreted antibodies
Pump lymph directly through the thoracic duct
Remove old red cells from splenic red pulp

questions.explanation: Helper cells coordinate B-cell differentiation and antibody responses.

questions.stem: Why is it misleading to say MHC I means 'this cell is infected'?

choices.text: Normal nucleated cells express MHC I; T cells evaluate the particular peptide displayed and activation context
MHC I occurs only on bacteria
MHC I is expressed exclusively by cells already dying
CD8 T cells bind every MHC I molecule and kill any such cell

questions.explanation: Class I MHC is normal self-identification and antigen presentation; recognition of disease-associated peptide matters.

questions.stem: Which cell directly secretes most antibodies during an active humoral response?

choices.text: Plasma cell
Naive CD8 T cell
Neutrophil
Red blood cell

questions.explanation: Plasma cells are specialized descendants of activated B cells.

questions.stem: How does a B-cell receptor initially recognize antigen compared with a T-cell receptor?

choices.text: It can bind native antigen, whereas a conventional TCR recognizes peptide presented by MHC
It recognizes MHC only, whereas TCR binds circulating chylomicrons
It never binds antigen until a plasma cell is formed
It recognizes only RNA inside the thymus

questions.explanation: BCR and TCR use distinct forms of antigen recognition.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is commonly dominant in serum and important for secondary systemic responses?

choices.text: IgG
IgE
IgD
IgA only

questions.explanation: IgG is a major circulating antibody class involved in diverse effector functions.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is commonly secreted early in a primary humoral response?

choices.text: IgM
IgD
IgE
IgA only

questions.explanation: IgM is usually an early secreted isotype in primary immune responses.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is especially important in mucus, saliva, and tears?

choices.text: IgA
IgM only
IgE only
IgD only

questions.explanation: Secretory IgA helps protect mucosal surfaces.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin participates prominently in immediate allergic responses?

choices.text: IgE
IgD
IgA
IgG exclusively

questions.explanation: Antigen-specific IgE on mast cells and basophils can trigger degranulation.

questions.stem: Which class commonly functions as an antigen receptor on mature naive B cells?

choices.text: IgD
IgE only
IgA only
Complement C3

questions.explanation: IgD is associated with the surface of naive mature B cells, often alongside IgM.

questions.stem: What is an epitope?

choices.text: A particular molecular site of an antigen recognized by an antibody or receptor
The entire thoracic duct
A germinal center made from red blood cells
A valve between two lymphangions

questions.explanation: The term antigenic determinant refers to the recognized site, not necessarily the whole pathogen.

questions.stem: Which type of immunity develops following vaccination?

choices.text: Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Nonspecific mechanical filtration only

questions.explanation: Vaccination elicits the recipient's own adaptive response and memory.

questions.stem: Which is an example of natural passive immunity?

choices.text: Maternal antibody transfer to an infant
Producing memory B cells after recovering from infection
Developing immunity after vaccination
Cytotoxic T-cell killing after antigen presentation

questions.explanation: Passive immunity transfers protective antibody from another individual.

questions.stem: Which is an example of artificial passive immunity?

choices.text: Administration of preformed antibodies to provide immediate protection
Standard vaccination using antigen to induce memory
Natural recovery from a viral infection
Creation of thymocytes in fetal bone marrow

questions.explanation: Passive immunization supplies antibodies rather than requiring an initial endogenous response.

questions.stem: Why is a secondary adaptive response often faster than a primary response?

choices.text: Previously formed memory lymphocytes and long-lived antibody responses can respond rapidly
Blood capillaries permanently become lymphatic vessels
The thymus directly secretes all antibody isotypes within seconds
It contains no antigen recognition steps

questions.explanation: Memory changes the starting state of a subsequent encounter.

questions.stem: What is measured by an antibody titer?

choices.text: Amount or functional activity of specific antibody in a specimen, often via serial dilution
Total number of lymph nodes in the body
Percentage of blood that is plasma
Width of a lymphatic valve

questions.explanation: Titer is an assay-dependent measurement of antibody.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes innate from adaptive immunity?

choices.text: Adaptive B/T responses are highly antigen-specific and can form memory; innate mechanisms respond rapidly via conserved pathways
Innate defenses are absent from vaccinated individuals
Adaptive immunity consists only of fever
Innate mechanisms always require a prior infection

questions.explanation: The difference concerns recognition, timing, and memory, not whether the two systems cooperate.

questions.stem: Why does advanced HIV infection weaken many immune responses?

choices.text: Loss/dysfunction of CD4 helper T cells disrupts coordination of adaptive immunity
HIV exclusively infects red blood cells and prevents oxygen transport
HIV removes lymphatic valves from the thoracic duct
HIV converts all B cells into neutrophils

questions.explanation: HIV targets CD4 T cells and causes progressive immune impairment without effective treatment.

questions.stem: What is autoimmunity?

choices.text: Immune responses damaging the body's own tissues
Normal removal of aged red blood cells by spleen
Production of chylomicrons after a meal
Migration of lymph through a node

questions.explanation: Autoimmune disorders result from failures in immune tolerance.
